In this Go repository (github.com/usememos/memos, at /bench/home/work), I need to find the function or method declared somewhere under the `internal/` directory that has the HIGHEST inbound call count (fan-in) — i.e., the exported (or even unexported) function/method under `internal/*` that is called from the most OTHER places across the entire codebase (server/, store/, cmd/, internal/ itself, etc.).

Approach:
1. First, list what packages exist under `internal/` (e.g., `internal/util`, `internal/log`, `internal/idp`, `internal/webhook`, `internal/storage`, `internal/httpgetter`, `internal/email`, `internal/markdown`, `internal/base`, etc. — check what's actually there with `ls` or `find`).
2. For each package, list its exported functions (public API surface) — these are the only ones plausibly callable from outside the package.
3. For the most likely candidates (utility functions like UUID generation, string/slice helpers, logging helpers, error wrapping, validation, ID generation, time helpers, etc.), grep the ENTIRE codebase for their usage count, e.g. `grep -rn "util\.SomeFunc(" --include=*.go | wc -l`.
4. Compare counts across candidates and identify the single highest one.

Pay special attention to small utility/helper packages under `internal/util` or similar — these tend to have the highest fan-in in codebases like this because things like UUID generation, string helpers, or pointer-to-value helpers get called everywhere.

Report the winning function/method's exact name, its declaring file (path:line), and an approximate count of call sites (grep count, roughly, distinguishing between actual call sites vs the declaration itself). Also list 2-3 runner-up candidates with their approximate counts for context.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: All much lower than the leaders. I now have enough data to report confidently.

## Findings: Highest fan-in function under `internal/`

**Winner (tied at the top, in production/non-test code): `util.GenUUID`**

- **Declaration:** `internal/util/util.go:40` — `func GenUUID() string { return uuid.New().String() }`
- **Call sites (non-test `.go` files):** 7 — `server/auth/token.go:194`, `server/router/api/v1/attachment_service_storage.go:209`, `server/router/api/v1/auth_service_session.go:26,135`, `server/router/api/v1/shortcut_service.go:154`, `server/router/api/v1/sso_username.go:15`, `server/router/api/v1/user_service_access_tokens.go:84`
- **If test files are included:** the count jumps to **28**, but 21 of those extra hits are boilerplate `tokenID := util.GenUUID()` lines repeated inside a single test file (`server/router/api/v1/test/auth_test.go`), so that inflated number reflects test repetition in one file rather than broad codebase fan-in.

**Co-leader: `filter.DefaultEngine`**

- **Declaration:** `internal/filter/engine.go:111` — `func DefaultEngine() (*Engine, error)`
- **Call sites:** 7, spread across genuinely distinct call sites in both `store/db/*` (sqlite/mysql/postgres memo & memo_relation queries) and `server/router/api/v1/shortcut_service.go:341`. No test-file inflation (all 7 are production code).

Given that `filter.DefaultEngine`'s 7 call sites are all distinct production call sites across three DB dialects plus the API layer (a more "real" cross-package fan-in signal), while `GenUUID`'s non-test count is also 7 but its test-inflated total is dominated by one repetitive test file, I'd call **`filter.DefaultEngine` (internal/filter/engine.go:111)** the more defensible single winner by genuine fan-in, with **`util.GenUUID` (internal/util/util.go:40)** as an essentially tied co-winner depending on whether you count test usage.

### Runner-up candidates

| Function | Declared at | Approx. call sites (non-test) |
|---|---|---|
| `filter.AppendConditions` | `internal/filter/helpers.go:9` | 6 (all in `store/db/{mysql,sqlite,postgres}/*.go`) |
| `util.ConvertStringToInt32` | `internal/util/util.go:14` | 5 (server/auth + server/router/api/v1/resource_name.go) |
| `filter.DefaultAttachmentEngine` | `internal/filter/engine.go:119` | 4 |
| `s3.NewClient` | `internal/storage/s3/s3.go:25` | 5 |

### Notes on why other "typical suspects" don't win
- `internal/util` also exposes `HasPrefixes`, `ValidateEmail`, `ReplaceString` — all **0** external call sites (essentially unused outside the package/tests).
- `internal/base` only defines a package-level var (`UIDMatcher`, a compiled regexp), not a function — it has 8 usages but isn't a function/method, so it's excluded from this ranking per the task's scope.
- Larger "framework-like" packages (`internal/markdown`, `internal/scheduler`, `internal/webhook`, `internal/email`, `internal/idp`) are consumed mostly through single service/interface instances (dependency-injected once), so their individual methods have low direct fan-in (1–4 call sites each), despite the packages being architecturally important.

Overall, fan-in for `internal/` functions in this codebase is modest (max ~7 genuine call sites) — there's no single utility function with runaway high fan-in like you might see in larger monorepos.
